chapter: Left out of the jazz books; Tatum, Handy and family
title: Putney Dandridge's bass lines at the Radio Inn
summary: At the Radio Inn on 18th Street, he heard Dandridge's beautiful piano bass lines, which influenced him.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: In other words kind of check up on the heritage, you know. I am very -- as you know, as I told you before -- chord conscious. But I have a -- you mentioned something to me that I had forgotten about working in Chicago with Elbert Topps.

Now, that was a club called the Radio Inn, I believe it was on 18th Street, and it was an after hours spot, and so on and so on. But I remember a guy came in one night who was there obviously with a show. He was a black guy, and his name was Putney Dandridge. This man made a tremendous impression upon me because he played piano and he had such beautiful bass lines. I had never heard this before.

Now, this guy -- I don't know, I haven't heard too much of him -- and I'm sure that there's a history, you know, a record of him, someplace. Putney Dandridge. But this guy had the most beautiful bass line on piano and it fascinated me. I never forgot it. And it influenced me quite a bit because I saw the beauty, you know. My mother always tried to tell me this, but here was a guy and I saw it with someone else. And he was a tremendous pianist. You see, but now the writers and the players now are very aware of bass lines, but this was done even then.
Oh, this was in the thirties, this was in the early thirties, you know.
Do you remember what show he was in?
I never knew. Only thing I remembered about him was his name. Because he impressed me that much. But there was Jelly Roll Morton, and J. P. Johnson, all of these were tremendous pianists. And they --
